strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP efficiency problem by jointly training low-rank adapters and quantization scales/offsets. Quantizing the merged weights offers a coherent way to avoid separate high-precision adapters at inference while reducing optimizer-state requirements relative to full QAT.

Table 2 provides encouraging evidence across five LLaMA/LLaMA 2 models and two bit widths: commonsense-task averages consistently exceed GPTQ+LoRA by 0.8–3.7 percentage points. The 4-bit results remain within 0.7 points of the full-precision LoRA baseline.

The manuscript provides algorithmic pseudocode, several training hyperparameters, initialization ablations, and a reported 33B training demonstration within 80 GB. These establish a useful experimental starting point.
weaknesses: The central memory-efficiency claims are not adequately isolated. L4Q uses BF16 optimizer states while baselines use FP32, and the approximately 29 GB reduction versus LoRA in Table 4 cannot be explained by changing optimizer precision for only 10.1M trainable parameters. Section 4.2 itself reports that BF16 LoRA fits the 33B model in 69.2 GB, versus 73.2 GB for L4Q. Table 1 also shows substantially higher memory than GPTQ+LoRA. Comparisons with matched precision and a breakdown of weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states are needed to establish the actual advantage.

The backward equations are inconsistent with the stated forward computation. Equations (8–9) omit the LoRA scaling factor alpha and do not specify how clipping affects adapter gradients. Equation (13), as written, omits the learned offset from the in-range scale derivative. The initialization parameter gamma mentioned in Section 4.1 is also undefined in the algorithm. These ambiguities affect reproduction of the core method and require corrected equations tied to the implementation.

The ablation does not cleanly establish the proposed mechanism. Table 4 assigns 56.7M trainable parameters to L4Q(s') and 113.4M to L4Q(s), although both are described as scale-only variants differing in initialization; L4Q(s,b) then has the same count as L4Q(s). These inconsistencies need resolution. A controlled comparison across optimizer precisions and scale/bias configurations is also necessary to support the claim that jointly learning both parameters enables reliable BF16 training.

Baseline coverage and training protocols limit the comparative conclusions. QA-LoRA appears only for LLaMA 7B commonsense evaluation, with no MMLU comparison; QLoRA and the cited LoftQ are not directly evaluated. Methods also use different training budgets and, for QA-LoRA, different group sizes. These differences do not invalidate the reported gains, but matched-budget experiments or learning curves are needed to substantiate convergence and efficiency advantages.

The MMLU discussion overstates the results. At 4 bits, LLaMA 13B L4Q scores below GPTQ+LoRA in both zero-shot evaluation (41.3 versus 42.1) and five-shot evaluation (44.3 versus 46.9). LLaMA 7B L4Q also declines from 33.5 zero-shot to 32.4 five-shot. The paper should distinguish these mixed findings from its consistent commonsense gains and report uncertainty for small differences.

Reproducibility and deployment evidence remain incomplete. The manuscript links underlying frameworks but supplies no L4Q implementation, and omits important memory-reproduction details such as microbatching and activation checkpointing. The 33B demonstration uses a sequence length of only 128. Quantized-weight storage during training is explicitly unimplemented, and integer-kernel inference acceleration is not measured. Together with the methodological inconsistencies above, these gaps prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present; targeted corrections and controlled experiments appear feasible for the next review cycle.
